title: The substituted words fit no one buried with Christ; sin is the devil
english: Since, then, the words spoken in character fit neither the inspired Paul nor anyone buried together with Christ through baptism—because such people have been freed from the so-called flesh—for such people will no longer be condemned because of Adam's disobedience; sin no longer reigns over them, nor the death that comes through sin. For they were buried together with the life of Christ, who obliterated disobedience by his obedience and drove out the death that came upon us from it by his voluntary death. For he willingly came under the law of disobedience, so that he might redeem us who were under the law of condemnation. For this reason every redeemed person says: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25). For what the law could not do, weakened as it was through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and he condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3).

That these things have been rightly understood in this way, the divine apostle shows by adding: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:1-2), and what follows these words.

Let me now attempt, briefly and in passing, to speak about the very words spoken in character, beginning from “But sin, having taken an occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me” (Romans 7:11). The name “sin” does not indicate a subsisting essence, but rather a manner and way of life of someone who has missed the mark of what is reasonable and right. For “sin” is a most general name, predicated of many different things. But every sin comes about neither by reason nor by a commanding law; for if it came about according to law and right reason, it would no longer be a sin, since it would have a defined and ordered principle of its coming into being.

Since, however, the divine apostle does not mention mere sins, but a most general sin having a mind, having a law, able to act craftily and to procure occasions for the construction of evil, he calls no other by the general name of sin than the originator and father of sins himself, the devil. For this reason the apostle also declared that he reigns over sins: “Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:12). For just as we call people by the craft they practice, so also he calls the devil himself “sin,” since he was the first inventor of sin.

Since, then, through the commandment given to Adam he deceived the man, and through it deceived Adam, procuring occasions through the commandment—and this is what he says: “Why is it that God said, ‘You shall not eat from any tree in the garden’? And on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:1, 5). He acts craftily, hiding the deception under a greater promise; he promises more, so that he may overturn the guardians of the commandment from the foundations of virtue by a fall like his own. For having goaded the man to want to become equal to God, he procured the occasion for his deceptive conversation from the commandment that had been given. For this reason Paul said: “But sin, having taken an occasion through the commandment, deceived me.”
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Didymus has just shown that the words of Romans 7 cannot belong to Paul or any Christian, and now he explains why: those buried with Christ are freed from the flesh, sin, and death, and the 'sin' that deceived through the commandment is the devil himself.

title: The commandment is holy; sin is not sin by nature but became sin beyond measure
english: So that no one would blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a neighboring and kindred word, saying: “We know that the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is not sin by nature and substance, he adds: “So that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment” (Romans 7:13). For what is something by substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is essentially. For what comes to be and accrues something to it, whether little or beyond measure, is other in substance than the things accruing to it. Quantity is not substance but is around the substance, not being substance. Therefore the one called sin by the apostle, admitting more sinning, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure—then it also received a beginning of being sin, insofar as it is sin, not being sinful beyond measure in the beginning, in accordance with its having sinned. Therefore he indicates the intensification of becoming sinful beyond measure in time to come, saying: “So that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment” (Romans 7:13). But if they say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just? How could they be holy, when through their occasion sin became sinful beyond measure? Let them hear in response that if something is harmed, the occasion through which it is harmed is not therefore already base and evil. For it is not because those who gaze at the sun improperly and without measure harm their eyes that we say the sun is evil; nor is it because the devil became sinful beyond measure by plotting against the Son of God that we say the Son of God is base and evil. “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18). Now he explains into the person of Adam. And because he was deprived of having God in himself, having exchanged true life for death—for not only the common death of his members took hold of him, but also the death of disobedience having invaded his soul. For the ruling death reigned especially before the coming of Christ, reigned over all, having disobedience as law and scepter of his own kingdom. But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for dying comes from the living, and the disobedience of someone arises from the obedience of those who obey. “For willing lies close to me, but working out the good does not. For the good I will, I do not do, but the evil I hate, this I practice” (Romans 7:18-19). If willing alone is in us, but working out the willed good is not in us, then the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain; for they do not do what is dear to him and to them, they do not enact it, but only will it—and perhaps not even that, for it is unclear.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Didymus is explaining Paul's words in Romans 7, arguing that the commandment and law are holy, just, and good, while 'sin' means the devil, who is not sin by nature but became sin beyond measure through the commandment.

title: The impious objection and the indwelling devil
english: But if this is true, I will speak according to the impious: then the good was not and will not be in life, nor did anyone ever work it, if they take the words “the good I will, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice” as the abolition of the good and noble in every human being. And from where were the names of virtues found in human life? But if there are those who work the good, even if those who do this are few, will not all make this claim: “We know that good does not dwell in us”? For the good they will, this they practice. But if those who work the good do so while existing in flesh, and those who do not do this but do evil are also in flesh, then the cause of the good not coming to be must not be attached to the flesh, but to the softness of soul of these people. For if evil dwells beside those who will to do the good, and likewise the good lies beside those who will to do evil, and having deliberated beforehand and willed beforehand they come to such a degree of activity, then our bodies are not evil by nature and substance. For deliberation and willing precede our actions, and these belong to a soul that has free will, able to incline toward whatever actions it wishes.

“But now it is no longer I who work it out, but the sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:17). Through this saying he has defended the point that the flesh is not evil by nature. For it is not the flesh we are clothed with that dwells in us, but the devil who dwells in the lawless. For in the same way that I say Christ dwells in every righteous person who works the good, in the same way I think the devil dwells in every evildoer. Therefore we are not evil insofar as we have flesh, but the sin dwelling in us is something other than the flesh and the soul of the human being. For the devil is said to sojourn especially in the soul, according to “Satan entered into the heart of Judas” (John 13:27), and according to “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart?” (Acts 5:3). And it is well said, “no longer I work it out, but the sin dwelling in me.” For there is a great distance between a work and a working out, because the working out precedes the work, as for example of a house or a ship; the working out is the preliminary preparation of the material. So the sin dwelling in those who sin—that is, Satan—admittedly works out beforehand in our reasonings the pattern of the coming evil, the preparation, while the soul that has received him cooperates with him in the evil, just as the womb of the female cooperates with those who sow for the sown seed to come to term. And since evil reasonings come out of the heart, from the conception of the devil that has occurred, the divine saying cries out: “destroying reasonings and every high thing lifted up against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:5). Just as the Holy Spirit is said to labor together with virtue-loving souls, according to “I labored more abundantly than all, yet not I but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10), so when a careless soul is persuaded by the devil’s urgings, it has the devil himself as a coworker toward evil. For he himself has worked out beforehand in it the pattern of the coming sin. For this reason it is said, “no longer I work it out, but the sin dwelling in me.”

u01-rem-close: the locked text reads οὐ καλὸν παράκειται; we translate as τὸ καλὸν παράκειται, because ὁμοίως and the parallel with Rom 7:21 (ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται) call for it. Taken literally, the transmitted text would say 'what is not good lies beside those who will to do evil.'
orientation: Didymus is answering an impious objection to Paul's words in Romans 7, arguing that the flesh is not evil by nature but that the devil dwelling in evildoers works out sin.
